rewrites.blindSummary:
This nation is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 2 years under Article 135) and, more fundamentally, this nation is one of the world's most closed nations: the government exerts strict media control and heavy internet monitoring, no independent research on LGBTI issues has been possible since 2019, and asylum is the community's most urgent need (an international LGBTI-rights organisation). An international human-rights organisation has documented systematic abuses. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, no recourse, and no visibility — the only safe strategy is total concealment.

For a visitor: any discoverable online presence or visible nonconformity is dangerous in a nation that monitors communications pervasively.
rewrites.blindTangential: Article 135 criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 2 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Absence of documentation is itself evidence of severity: data collection is impossible because it is unsafe.
blindSourceSummaries: An international LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2025 (covering 2024): the April 2022 criminal code not only kept the 'sodomy' provisions but increased both the severity and scope of punishments; torture and inhumane treatment remain present throughout the nation with relatives reporting LGBTI people subjected to them — the current penal-risk read.

A foreign government's 2021 human-rights report on this nation: lists among significant human-rights issues the existence of laws criminalising consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults, alongside officials in security services committing abuses and engaging in corruption with impunity — official assessment of law plus enforcement climate.

A stakeholder mid-term review submission (2020): LGBT persons and people living with HIV in this nation 'have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights'; identifies article 135 of the criminal code criminalising consensual same-sex acts between adult men as the core foundation of profound systemic discrimination, and notes increasing flight abroad.

A regional legislative analysis (2019, 11 pages): maps the legal landscape and barriers for LGBT people and people living with HIV — deliberately compiled so NGOs, community activists and government can use it when planning advocacy; the standing legal-baseline reference for the nation.

A university law clinic (May 1, 2007): secured asylum in a foreign nation for an anonymous woman persecuted because she is a lesbian and for her political opinions — believed to be the first-ever asylum granted to a lesbian from this nation; documents persecution grounds cited by people fleeing the nation.

A law firm (September 2019): attorneys secured asylum for a lesbian couple from this nation who feared persecution including imprisonment and torture; homosexuality is punishable by up to 2 years; suspects face interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals; women are vulnerable to sexual violence and 'honor killings'.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This nation is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Articles 520/517 of the Penal Code criminalise 'sexual acts against nature' and public indecency; there is no legal gender recognition. Since the fall of the former government (December 2024), the situation has worsened: a monitoring organisation documented 'waves of violence' against transgender women in the first two months of 2025, implicating both armed groups outside the government and security forces in multiple cities, and February 2025 videos showed authorities arresting trans women. Digital targeting (entrapment via apps, extortion) is documented across the conflict period.

For a visitor: active conflict, trans-targeted violence waves, no recourse whatsoever.
rewrites.blindTangential: Articles 520/517 criminalise 'sexual acts against nature' — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: General conflict risk affects all; the 2025 trans-women violence waves are trans-specific.
blindSourceSummaries: A monitoring organisation's report of April 2025: working through an on-the-ground reporter network, the organisation investigated and found inaccurate a report claiming LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted and targeted in a city, debunking it to avoid stirring incitement against the community.
thin: no usable finding

An international LGBTI-rights organisation's overview of this nation (updated 12 March 2026): this nation's legal landscape remains highly restrictive — Penal Code Articles 520 ('acts against nature') and 517 (public indecency) criminalise same-sex conduct for both men and women; legal gender recognition impossible; LGBTI organisations cannot register.

A human-rights organisation's report of 16 April 2018 (updated 30 August 2021): documents LGBT activism across the region including this nation, with tallies that an armed group claimed at least 16 killings in this nation for alleged sodomy as of June 2016 (23 elsewhere, 3 elsewhere); activists worked to draw attention to the killings including at the international security council.

A news feature of 11 October 2020: LGBT people from this nation describe life at home and abroad — in the capital, homosexuality and 'public decency' offences are illegal, and a 36-year-old describes living 'only in whispers' when meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes.

A news outlet (2015): two gay refugees from this nation and another nation testified at the first-ever meeting on LGBT rights at the international security council — a closed session co-sponsored by two foreign governments — about the constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and armed groups.

A news outlet, 23 June 2010: authorities in this nation raided several private gay parties over preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men in the latest swoop — most charged with 'homosexual acts', others with dealing or buying drugs.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This nation is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The Penal Code criminalises 'illicit sexual intercourse' and 'indecent acts' (up to 5 years), and a monitoring organisation documents de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and transition through these provisions — compounded by recent religious rulings declaring the very term 'gender' religiously impermissible, making anyone using it in media or institutions susceptible to prosecution. Militias control regions and operate detention sites where torture is systematic; there is no functioning central judiciary, no legal gender recognition, and no protection of any kind.

For a visitor: detention by any of several militia authorities is the modal bad outcome, with no consular reach in much of the nation.
rewrites.blindTangential: 'Illicit sexual intercourse' and 'indecent acts' provisions (up to 5 years) capture same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity alike.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Militia fragmentation means enforcement varies by region; the trans-specific mechanism is documented de-facto criminalisation.
blindSourceSummaries: A monitoring organisation's review of this nation: this nation has de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and of the transition process (social, medical, surgical), enforced through 'indecent acts' and 'illicit intercourse' provisions; recent religious rulings have designated gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible.

An international LGBTI-rights organisation's overview (updated 12 March 2026): same-sex relations not legal for men or women; 'indecent acts' provisions carry up to 5 years' imprisonment; no legal protections against discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity; same-sex relationships not legally recognised; legal gender recognition unavailable (official identity documents cannot be changed); LGBTI organisations cannot register.

A news outlet's guide (21 June 2016): this nation is among regional nations where homosexuality carries imprisonment as the penalty (specific terms vary by nation); where no specific law exists, other laws are used — the guide assesses the catastrophic effect of these regimes on gay people's lives.

A human-rights organisation (8 June 2015): documents an armed group's killing of men accused of homosexuality in areas it controlled, including a city in this nation — a young man there was targeted by local militants for effeminate dress and 'contemporary' clothes (case named from November 2014).

A news outlet (June 2015): militants executed three young men accused of homosexual acts in a city in April 2015; the piece reports information in that city flows only through the mosque and concludes the situation for homosexuals in this nation is getting worse as militias control regions.

A news outlet (26 November 2012): 12 men accused of being gay faced torture and threatened death at the hands of a local militia — early post-revolutionary vigilante violence against suspected gay men.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This nation is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The legal framework criminalises same-sex conduct (up to death under some interpretations of the Penal Code; 100 lashes/1 year otherwise), but a monitoring organisation emphasises the operative mechanism: the erosion of the rule of law and the power of militias has facilitated a surge in attacks targeting transgender individuals — de facto criminalisation operating outside any judicial system. Areas controlled by one armed movement impose their own moral-policing regime; other areas have their own militia authorities.

For a visitor: no safe authority to appeal to anywhere in the nation.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to death under some interpretations; 100 lashes/1 year otherwise) — a catastrophic exposure for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: War risk affects all; the documented surge in trans-targeted attacks is trans-specific.
blindSourceSummaries: A monitoring organisation's review of this nation: erosion of the rule of law plus humanitarian crisis and growing militia influence mean de-facto criminalisation is rarely enforced but is used to justify civilians taking matters into their own hands (vigilante risk); critically, the penal provisions apply ONLY in government-controlled regions — other areas sit under different factions in the ongoing conflict, so legal exposure varies by region.

A human-rights organisation's report (16 April 2018, regional): this nation is one of 14 covered nations where zina provisions criminalise sex outside marriage and same-sex acts are explicitly prohibited; the report could identify NO activists in this nation willing to speak about their work (a documented safety gap), and notes 'breach of modesty' laws used against expression.

A human-rights organisation's world report 2026 chapter on this nation (events of 2025): its sexual-orientation-and-gender-identity section states this nation's penal code prohibits same-sex relations — Article 264 punishes anal sex with 100 lashes and one year in prison if participants are not married, with the article prescribing differently if married — alongside a world's-worst humanitarian crisis (tens of millions needing aid) and factional control between an armed movement and the government affecting where law applies.

An international human-rights organisation (February 2024): two courts run by an armed movement in this nation sentenced more than 40 people to death, flogging or prison over same-sex conduct — one court (23 January) sentenced nine to death (seven by stoning, two by crucifixion) with 23 more given 6 months to 10 years for 'homosexuality'/'spreading immorality', and another court (1 February) handed further death sentences; the organisation demanded an immediate halt.

A legal-reference website's laws page for this nation: consensual same-sex sex is unlawful under Penal Code 1994 Article 264 — homosexuality between men defined as anal penetration; unmarried men punishable with 100 lashes (and up to one year's imprisonment per the statute); the canonical statute citation for this nation's criminalisation.

A news outlet (16 August 2013): the capital's social climate — a gay man describes hiding (hood over long hair) as 'still problematic'; conservative society has no place for them while the law sees homosexuality as punishable by death; illustrates discretionary-social enforcement layered on the statutory penalty.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This nation is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021 — a genuine turning point — and LGBTIQ organisations can now register and operate legally. The government engages with a United Nations agency's equality campaign at the level of the highest court and the cabinet. Trans women report violence and discrimination remain widespread (trans people four times more likely to experience assault), and there is no legal gender recognition, but there is no criminalisation, no police targeting pattern, and a national culture that discourages open aggression.

Tourism is tightly regulated (a daily fee system), which incidentally provides visitors a structured, monitored environment.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2021 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: No legal gender recognition — resident-facing; the four-times assault likelihood and violence/discrimination reports describe residents' experience.
blindSourceSummaries: An international LGBTI-rights organisation's overview of this nation (updated 12 March 2026): consensual same-sex intimacy decriminalised in 2021, but there is no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit protections on sexual orientation or gender identity; LGBTIQ organisations may register, though activists call the process lengthy and burdensome. Legal gender recognition is unavailable — earlier administrative gender-marker changes are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines. Discrimination and stigma persist, especially in health-care access.

A national broadcaster (November 2024): trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault; a 49-year-old trans woman describes having nowhere to report violence — police dismiss her cases because her identity card reads male ('both parties are men'), families pressure victims to accept it as fate, and help routed through the LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. Practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

A United Nations agency's report (31 March 2025, 37 pages): the 2024 equality campaign trained the highest court, the office of the top government lawyer and the cabinet secretariat, and secured the first-ever direct dialogue between this nation's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians; two consultation workshops convened community members with United Nations and national children-and-women commission representatives.

A news site (10 June 2019): this nation's lower house voted 43-1 to repeal Penal Code Sections 213-214 'unnatural sex' provisions (1 month to 1 year, unenforced for at least 15 years); upper-house ratification still pending at that point.

A news site (11 March 2021): the Penal Code Amendment Act came into force 17 February 2021 — after the upper house reinserted the ban, a December 2020 joint sitting clarified that 'homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex', completing decriminalisation (the global count of criminalising nations fell from 72 to 71). A later freshness review confirms this stands with no post-2021 reversal.

A national broadcaster's feature: an online community page (from around 2014) produced this nation's first public affirmation of a gay population; profiles the page's admins and one of only two trans women living publicly, who at 16 fought to wear the female school uniform — a first in this nation's society. Public trans visibility exists but remains exceptional.

A news outlet (28 October 2015): this nation's LGBT people report very little persecution or violence but near-total social invisibility — growing up gay was described as a very alienating experience, with no shared language for gay or trans identities and lesbianism under-recognised. A prominent public LGBT figure founded the online community page in 2013.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This nation demands real caution from trans visitors. Courts have delivered important rulings (the 2023 recognition of foreign same-sex marriages; earlier document-change wins for trans people), but same-sex conduct between men technically remains criminalised under the common law (the 2024 high court declined to strike it, and parliament passed hostile marriage bills), and implementation of pro-LGBT rulings is documented as unsatisfactory (by a regional legal organisation). The capital has a small organised community; police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

For a visitor: enforcement of the old law is essentially nil, but the legal floor is hostile and the politics are deteriorating.
rewrites.blindTangential: Male same-sex conduct technically remains criminalised under the common law (unenforced) — a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2024 legislative backlash signals trajectory.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The earlier document-change court wins are per-case resident litigation; implementation gaps documented by a regional legal organisation are resident-facing.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Common-law criminalisation is unenforced but real; implementation gaps are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: An op-ed (22 May 2024) by two lawyers of a regional legal organisation: the supreme court in May 2023 ordered the government to recognise same-sex marriages concluded abroad under the immigration act, but compliance has failed — immigration officials tell the litigant himself that the ruling covers only case couples (he receives a visitor's visa on every exit), and gender-recognition orders are applied only to named applicants rather than all persons. A hostile parliamentary marriage-bill response and misleading media amplified the non-implementation. Documents the enforcement gap between pro-equality rulings and administrative practice.

A regional development programme report (December 2024): regional framework document; this nation's courts have decriminalised same-sex conduct (2024) and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, though implementation remains contested.

A regional legal organisation's report (2017): constitutional analysis — the constitution's equality article omits gender identity or sexual orientation but 'other status' should include them per the international human-rights committee; section 7B of the births, marriages and deaths registration act 81 of 1963 allows gender-marker changes on medical evidence, handled case-by-case and 'not problematic' per a legal assistance centre.

A news outlet (28 May 2018): an LGBTI organisation opened this nation's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre on 17 May — HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, mental and sexual/reproductive health services, with plans for legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations. The organisation's director said: 'It is a first.' The article notes the historic-era sodomy law is on the books but not believed used since independence, and recalls 2016 international human-rights committee recommendations urging non-discrimination legislation.

A news outlet (12 December 2018): dozens marched in two cities on 8 December for LGBTI+ Pride — described as the 'biggest pride event' to date in this nation. Dated evidence of a visible, tolerated public community presence.

A news outlet (26 June 2014): a local version of a neighbouring nation's political movement was launched with identical branding (T-shirts, berets) but an explicitly anti-gay stance, unlike the original. Documents organised political hostility to LGBT rights in this nation's political environment.
